topics.title: Production debugging — what evidence do you need beyond a console error?
topics.html:
A useful production report connects a failure to a release, a route or operation, and the steps that produced it. A minified stack without context rarely explains the whole incident.

  • Associate errors and timings with an application release and a normalized operation name. Correlate frontend requests with server request IDs when the system provides them.
  • Distinguish a transport failure, an HTTP error, a payload-validation error, and a rendering failure. Their fixes and retry behavior differ.
  • Source maps map generated code back to source locations. They must correspond to the exact deployed artifact, not merely a similar branch checkout.
  • Measure the phase you mean. A timer around fetch and JSON parsing does not establish when React committed the result or the browser painted it.

Keep telemetry intentional: capture enough context to diagnose behavior without logging whole user payloads by default. If source maps should not be publicly served, upload matching maps to the error-reporting system as part of the release process.

async function loadCatalog() {
  // Local names keep simultaneous operations from sharing these marks.
  const id = crypto.randomUUID();
  const start = `catalog:${id}:start`;
  const end = `catalog:${id}:end`;
  const measureName = `catalog:${id}:request-and-parse`;
  performance.mark(start);
  try {
    const response = await fetch('/api/catalog');
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}`);
    return await response.json();
  } finally {
    performance.mark(end);
    const measure = performance.measure(measureName, start, end);
    console.log({ operation: 'catalog:request-and-parse', durationMs: measure.duration });
    performance.clearMarks(start);
    performance.clearMarks(end);
    performance.clearMeasures(measureName);
  }
}
In plain words

I first make the failure identifiable: which release, which operation, and which boundary failed. Then I use matching source maps and targeted timings to investigate a concrete event rather than collecting an unexplained error message.

Does hiding source maps make frontend logic secret?
No. Executable client code is still delivered to the browser. Map visibility controls how easily source locations and original source content are exposed; it is not an authorization mechanism.
Should I swallow an error after reporting it?
Only if the application has a defined recovery path. Reporting and handling are separate decisions; swallowing a failed operation can leave the screen pretending it completed successfully.
Official references
  • Chrome DevTools: JavaScript source maps
  • MDN: Performance.measure

topics.title: A tab gets slower after every navigation — how do you prove a memory leak?
topics.html:
A leak keeps objects reachable after the application no longer needs them. A temporarily high allocation rate or a cache with a deliberate bound is not automatically a leak.

  • Reproduce a repeatable cycle: enter a screen, perform the same action, leave it, and repeat.
  • Compare heap snapshots or allocation recordings and inspect retaining paths. Look for surviving subscriptions, timers, detached DOM nodes, and closures retaining large graphs.
  • Check whether caches have a size or lifetime bound. Accumulating every search response indefinitely may be the retention policy itself.
  • Garbage collection is nondeterministic. A value not disappearing immediately after one unmount does not by itself prove that it can never be collected.

Fix the owner and lifetime of the retained resource, then repeat the same measurement. JavaScript heap analysis is only one view: image, GPU, worker, or native memory can require additional tools, especially in a mobile application.

import { useEffect, useState } from 'react';

export function TickCounter() {
  const [ticks, setTicks] = useState(0);

  useEffect(() => {
    const timer = setInterval(() => {
      setTicks(previous => previous + 1);
    }, 1000);

    return () => clearInterval(timer);
  }, []);

  return <p>{ticks} ticks</p>;
}
// The timer belongs to this mounted component, not the whole tab lifetime.
In plain words

I do not diagnose a leak from one large number. I repeat a lifecycle, find what survives, and follow the references keeping it alive. The fix belongs to the resource’s owner, followed by the same before-and-after measurement.

Does using WeakMap automatically fix a leaking design?
No. It helps only when weakly held keys match the ownership model. A global listener, pending task, or separate strong reference can still retain the same objects.
Can DevTools affect what stays alive during investigation?
Yes. Inspecting or logging objects can retain them through the debugging environment. Be deliberate about the reproduction and inspect retaining paths rather than assuming every reference came from application code.
Official references
  • Chrome DevTools: memory problems
  • Chrome DevTools: heap snapshots

topics.title: Dates, instants, and time zones — why is a calendar date appearing a day earlier?
topics.html:
An instant and a calendar date are different domain values. A JavaScript Date represents a timestamp; it does not permanently carry the display time zone the user originally selected.

  • Exchange instants in an unambiguous form, such as an ISO timestamp with an offset or Z, and format them in an explicit display zone when the requirement needs one.
  • A date-only string such as 2026-10-21 is interpreted as UTC by the Date parser. Local formatting in a zone behind UTC can show the previous calendar day.
  • A birthday or delivery date may be a calendar date without an instant. Do not automatically convert every date-only field into midnight UTC.
  • For future appointments tied to local wall time, preserve the relevant time-zone intent and define how daylight-saving gaps or repeated times are resolved.

Use Intl for presentation. Avoid hand-built offset arithmetic and assumptions that a local day always has 24 elapsed hours. Validate invalid dates and test the boundary between the server’s zone, the product’s zone, and the viewer’s zone.

const instant = new Date('2026-10-21T10:00:00Z');
if (Number.isNaN(instant.getTime())) throw new Error('Invalid timestamp');

const formatter = new Intl.DateTimeFormat('en-GB', {
  timeZone: 'Europe/Warsaw',
  dateStyle: 'medium',
  timeStyle: 'short',
});
console.log(formatter.format(instant));

// A calendar-only domain value can stay a validated date string:
const deliveryDate = '2026-10-21';
// Its meaning is not "an instant at midnight UTC" unless the contract says so.
In plain words

I decide whether the value means a point on the global timeline or a date on someone’s calendar. Mixing those meanings is what produces many one-day shifts and daylight-saving bugs.

Can I parse any localized date with new Date(text)?
No. Arbitrary display formats are not a portable input contract. Use an explicit input format and parser rather than depending on browser-specific interpretation.
Can I add 24 hours to get the same local time tomorrow?
That is an elapsed-time operation, which can differ from a local-calendar operation around a daylight-saving transition. Choose the operation that matches the business requirement and test the relevant zone.
Official references
  • MDN: Date
  • MDN: Intl.DateTimeFormat

topics.title: Money and localization — why is toFixed(2) not a complete currency model?
topics.html:
Separate the domain amount, the currency, the rounding policy, and its localized display. They are not interchangeable strings.

  • Binary floating-point cannot exactly represent many decimal fractions. For bounded amounts, integer minor units can make addition straightforward; more demanding calculations may require an exact decimal model.
  • Do not assume every currency has two minor-unit digits. Keep the currency code and use the contract appropriate to that currency.
  • Intl.NumberFormat supplies locale-aware grouping, decimal separators, signs, and currency placement. It formats a value; it does not establish correct business arithmetic.
  • Define when rounding occurs: per item, per tax line, or on a total can produce different results. The authoritative pricing contract must be consistent across client and server.

Do not use a formatted currency string as the stored amount or feed arbitrary localized input to parseFloat. Formatting and parsing are different tasks, and large integer or decimal values still require deliberate bounds and precision handling.

// This example specifically models USD, which has two minor-unit digits.
const itemMinor = 1299;
const shippingMinor = 250;
const totalMinor = itemMinor + shippingMinor;

const display = new Intl.NumberFormat('en-US', {
  style: 'currency',
  currency: 'USD',
}).format(totalMinor / 100);

console.log(display); // $15.49
// A multi-currency model must not hardcode /100 for every currency.
In plain words

I calculate using an explicit amount and currency model, then format the result for the person reading it. A string with two decimal places does not solve precision, currency rules, or where rounding is supposed to happen.

Can Intl.NumberFormat convert one currency into another?
No. It changes presentation, not economic value. Currency conversion requires a rate, a time or quote context, and a rounding policy supplied by the relevant system.
Can the client be the final authority for an order total?
The UI can calculate a useful preview, but the server must independently establish the accepted price, discounts, currency, and totals. A client-supplied number is not an authoritative pricing decision.
Official references
  • MDN: Intl.NumberFormat
  • MDN: Number and precision
